Krichene and Rendle show that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model orderings relative to full-catalog metrics, even in expectation; repeated sampling does not remove this bias. With 99 negatives, HR@10 measures performance within a 100-item candidate set, not full-catalog HR@10. Preserve the pinned evaluator and describe results explicitly as sampled HR@10; their proposed metric corrections would change the benchmark objective. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

Suggested uncertainty protocol: if per-user hit indicators are available, compare models on identical users and candidate sets. Bootstrap paired user outcomes within each category, resampling 200 users with replacement, then average the four category-level HR differences equally. Report the observed macro difference and a 95% bootstrap interval, using a separate fixed resampling seed without changing training or evaluation seeds. This estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on fitted models and fixed candidates; it does not capture training variability or negative-sampling bias. Paired resampling preserves correspondence between model outcomes. [SciPy bootstrap documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html)

Repeatedly selecting architectures or checkpoints against the same validation set creates selection optimism. Ordinary paired intervals calculated after selecting the winner do not correct that adaptive search. Predeclare the search budget, comparison baseline and selection rule; log all trials, treat validation intervals as exploratory, and reserve the host’s untouched final evaluation for the selected model. Re-evaluating identical predictions with the same evaluator seed supplies no independent evidence. [Cawley and Talbot, 2010](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
